title: Sodium Disorders — Hypo- & Hypernatremia
sources: Critical Vector — EM Pocket Guide: Sodium Disorders
ESC/ESE/ERBP hyponatremia guidance (2014, 2023 update); standard ICU electrolyte management

changelog.change: Initial entry — hyponatremia severity-based management with 3% NaCl dosing, ODS-prevention correction limits + the DDAVP/D5W rescue, SIADH criteria, hypernatremia classification, the free-water-deficit formula, and ICU sodium drift.

summary: In symptomatic hyponatraemia give 3% NaCl 100–150 mL IV over ~20 min (repeat ×2), targeting +4–6 mEq/L in the first hour to stop the emergency — then STOP and go slow. Overcorrection is the dangerous complication: re-lower with DDAVP + D5W if you exceed 8–10 mEq/L in 24 h.

rows: Treat the underlying cause; fluid-restrict to 500–1000 mL/day if SIADH
3% NaCl 100–150 mL IV over 20 min; may repeat ×2; target +4–6 mEq/L over the first hour
any Na⁺ with severe CNS signs
3% NaCl 150 mL IV bolus; repeat ×2 PRN until symptoms resolve; then STOP the rapid correction

body.text: Seizure in hyponatraemia: give 3% NaCl 150 mL IV bolus immediately regardless of the baseline Na⁺ — correct until the seizure stops, then slow down aggressively.

items: ≤ 8 mEq/L in any 24 h (some sources allow 10–12 in average-risk patients; 8 is the safer default). ≤ 18 mEq/L cumulative over 48 h.
Lower ceiling — ≤ 8 mEq/L/24 h — in high ODS risk: chronic hyponatraemia, alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, advanced liver disease, hypokalaemic states.
Overcorrected (> 8–10 mEq/L in 24 h): re-lower with DDAVP 1–2 mcg IV + D5W IV. Relowering is SAFE if done promptly.

Osmotic demyelination (ODS / central pontine myelinolysis) manifests 2–6 days AFTER the overcorrection — dysarthria, dysphagia, flaccid then spastic quadriparesis, 'locked-in'. Prevention is the only effective strategy.
Urine Na⁺ > 40 mEq/L (renal salt wasting) on a normal salt/water intake.
Normal thyroid, adrenal, and renal function; no recent diuretic.

body.text: Beer potomania / 'tea-and-toast' hyponatraemia: severe hyponatraemia with a VERY LOW urine osmolality (< 100) — low solute intake limits free-water excretion. It corrects fast once solute is given, so it's a high ODS-risk scenario — anticipate autocorrection and be ready with DDAVP.

rows: GI losses, diuretics, insensible losses — ISOTONIC saline first to restore perfusion, then switch to D5W or 0.45% NaCl once haemodynamically stable
Central DI (lack of ADH) or nephrogenic DI (ADH resistance) — D5W or 0.45% NaCl; DDAVP 1–4 mcg IV/SC q12–24 h for central DI
Iatrogenic (NaHCO₃ infusion, hypertonic-saline overuse) — D5W + furosemide to excrete the free-water-poor volume

body.text: Free water deficit (L) = 0.6 × TBW(kg) × [(Na⁺ / 140) − 1] (use 0.5 for women/elderly). Replace over 48–72 h; maximum rate of Na⁺ decline 0.5 mEq/L/hr (≤ 10–12/24 h) — faster risks cerebral oedema. Add ongoing and insensible losses to the deficit.

'ICU sodium drift': hypernatraemia develops insidiously in intubated patients from inadequate free water in tube feeds, hyperosmolar IV fluids, or excess insensible losses. A daily free-water balance review prevents it.

buildNote: Tier 1 — previously a gap. Cross-links the existing corrected-sodium and free-water-deficit calculators. A rapid hypertonic-saline dosing calculator (mL of 3% for a target ΔNa) is a natural companion.
